newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says may allow Timor Nobel laureate visit.
newsitem.headline: Manila says may allow Timor Nobel laureate visit.

text.p: The Philippines will allow East Timorese Nobel laureate Jose Ramos-Horta to enter the country if the government is consulted before the visit, President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday.
The government said earlier it had denied entry to the self-exiled East Timorese independence activist on the recommendation of a Cabinet committee on the basis of "national interest.

"There was no consultation. We were just reading in the newspapers that he (Ramos-Horta) is coming and there is a local non-government organisation that is hosting a conference to which he has been invited to be guest speaker," Ramos said.
"National interest must be served if there is a mutually agreed time to visit which must be based on some preliminary consultations," he told reporters at his weekly news conference.
The Manila Times newspaper said the decision to deny entry to Ramos-Horta was taken to avoid embarrassing Indonesia, a close ally of the Philippines.
Ramos-Horta, an outspoken campaigner for freedom for the Indonesia-ruled territory of East Timor, was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize along with East Timorese Bishop Carlos Belo.

The Philippines previously blocked Ramos-Horta, who lives in in Australia, from entering the country in November last year during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit. Both the Philippines and Indonesia are APEC members.
The palace said Ramos-Horta had applied for a visa to attend a human rights seminar which began in Manila on Tuesday and runs until January 28.
The Philippine Alliance of Human Rights Advocates, one of the conference organisers, said: "We cannot find any excuse for the government except that maybe it is being overly paranoid.
"It needs to shed off its martial law habit of suspecting all those who struggle for democratic aspirations as rebels and terrorists," the group said in a statement.

Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it a year later. The United Nations does not recognise Jakarta as the ruler of the territory and still considers Portugal the administering power.
